intro: This course has met the Watchers, the giants, the gods of the nations and the council of heaven. Where do those ideas come from? This unit goes to the sources. It opens the ancient documents themselves: 1 Enoch and Jubilees, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Josephus and Philo, the tablets of Ugarit and the traditions of Mesopotamia. Then it listens to the researchers who have spent their careers reading them.

The first chapter reads the documents. You will see what 1 Enoch 6–16 says about the Watchers on Mount Hermon, how Jubilees retells the story with Mastema and his spirits, and what the broken Book of Giants adds. You will read how Josephus and Philo explained Genesis 6 to Greek readers, and compare the council of El at Ugarit with Psalm 82. You will also learn Samuel Sandmel's warning against overstating parallels.

The second chapter joins the conversation among scholars: Mullen and Smith on the divine council, the text critics on Deuteronomy 32:8, Milik, VanderKam and Nickelsburg on the date of 1 Enoch, Wright and Stuckenbruck on evil spirits, Reed on how the story traveled, Segal on two powers in heaven, and Heiser on the three rebellions. By the end you will be able to state an argument fairly and tell a settled claim from an open one.
bigQuestion: What do the primary documents say about the Watchers and the council of heaven, and how do researchers read them differently?

timeline.t: Scribes at Ugarit write poems about El and the assembly of the gods
Berossus, a Babylonian priest, tells of the sage Oannes in Greek
Scribes copy parts of 1 Enoch in Aramaic; copies later found at Qumran
The Book of Jubilees retells Genesis with the Watchers and Mastema
Josephus finishes Jewish Antiquities in Rome
James Bruce brings Ge'ez copies of 1 Enoch to Europe
R. H. Charles's translations of 1 Enoch and Jubilees appear in a small English edition
A farmer's plow strikes a tomb near Ras Shamra, leading to Ugarit
The first Dead Sea Scrolls are found near Qumran
J. T. Milik publishes the Aramaic Enoch fragments from Cave 4
George Nickelsburg publishes his commentary on 1 Enoch
Annette Yoshiko Reed and Archie Wright publish studies of the Watchers' reception

words.d: the ancient document itself, such as a scroll, a tablet or a book of the Bible
a later writing that studies a primary source, such as a commentary or scholarly book
in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings who came down to earth and broke God's order
a collection of five ancient Jewish writings in Enoch's name; canonical in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
a Jewish retelling of Genesis and early Exodus from the second century BCE
in Jubilees, the chief of the spirits, who asks God to let a tenth of them remain
an assembly of heavenly beings around a chief god, found at Ugarit and, many scholars argue, in the Bible
in Mesopotamian tradition, seven wise beings before the flood who taught the arts of civilization
Samuel Sandmel's 1961 word for overstating likenesses between texts and assuming borrowing
the careful comparison of manuscripts to find the most likely earliest wording
how later readers took up, used and changed an earlier text
the facts that are hardest for a claim to explain

test.q: Which is a primary source for the Watchers story?
test.why: 1 Enoch is the ancient document itself; the others are secondary sources about it.

test.q: According to 1 Enoch 6, where did the Watchers swear their oath?
test.why: 1 Enoch 6 says the two hundred came down on the summit of Mount Hermon.

test.q: Which book says the Watchers were first sent to teach justice?
test.why: Jubilees 4:15 says they came down to teach and do uprightness, and fell later.

test.q: In Jubilees 10, what share of the spirits is left with Mastema?
test.why: Jubilees 10:9 leaves one tenth with Mastema and sends nine parts to judgment.

test.q: Which scholar edited the Qumran Book of Giants fragments in 1997?
test.why: Stuckenbruck's The Book of Giants from Qumran appeared in 1997.

test.q: To what did Josephus compare the sons born in Genesis 6?
choices: The sons of El at Ugarit
test.why: Antiquities 1.73 compares them with the giants of Greek stories.

test.q: Which Hebrew phrase in Psalm 82:1 matches Ugaritic language for the assembly of the gods?
test.why: Adat el, the council of El, closely matches Ugaritic council phrases.

test.q: Whose 2010 article compared the Mesopotamian apkallu with the Watchers?
test.why: Annus published On the Origin of Watchers in 2010.

test.q: What did Samuel Sandmel warn against in 1961?
choices: Comparing any two texts at all
test.why: Sandmel's word parallelomania names overdone comparisons.

test.q: Which reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 do most text critics now prefer?
test.why: A Qumran scroll and the Septuagint support sons of God.

test.q: Which part of 1 Enoch has not been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls?
test.why: No Parables fragments were found; their date is still debated.

test.q: Which scholar compared Enoch, seventh from Adam, with the Mesopotamian king Enmeduranki?
test.why: VanderKam made the comparison in Enoch and the Growth of an Apocalyptic Tradition (1984).

test.q: What reading of Genesis 6 did Julius Africanus and Augustine discuss?
test.why: The Sethite view reads the sons of God as Seth's line.

test.q: What did Heiser argue about the demons of the Gospels?
choices: They are the spirits of the dead giants, following 1 Enoch 15
They are the sons of Seth
test.why: In The Unseen Realm and Demons, Heiser traced them to 1 Enoch 15; other readers see fallen angels.

test.q: Which of these is still debated among scholars?
choices: Whether Genesis 3, 6 and 11 form three rebellions
Whether Ugarit's tablets are older than Qumran's
Whether 1 Kings 22 has a council scene
test.why: The three-rebellions framework is debated; the others are widely accepted.

write.prompt: Where does 1 Enoch say evil spirits come from, and how have researchers read it? Cite 1 Enoch 15:8–10, Jubilees 10:1–9 and Mark 1:23–27. Explain what each text says, then compare at least two researchers' readings, with evidence and counter-evidence.
tips: Start with the documents: say what each passage says before saying how anyone reads it.
Name each text by book, chapter and verse, and the translation you used.
Attribute every reading to its reader: Wright argues, Heiser held, many Christian readers think.
Give each reading's strongest evidence and its hardest counter-evidence.
Use the unit's terms, such as Watchers, Mastema, reception and primary source.
